articles.title: How to build your social media team for the future of marketing
articles.fullContent:
It’s certainly not 2010 anymore. So why are so many businesses still resourcing social media teams as if it is?

Social teams have evolved far beyond publishing posts and responding to comments. Today, they manage content and video production, influencer partnerships, customer care, social search, paid media, community engagement and increasingly, social intelligence. Social’s role is expanding across the business, and a social team’s structure needs to evolve with it.

Organizations are also looking to social data for more than marketing insights. According to Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report, 93% of leaders view social intelligence as essential for future growth, yet only 10% of organizations have embedded it into enterprise strategy. Closing that gap requires more support for social teams that are already stretched across a growing list of responsibilities. They need the right people, roles and processes to turn social data into action across the business while creating more capacity for strategic work.

There’s no one-size-fits-all social media team structure. But the strongest teams connect their work directly to business outcomes rather than organizing solely around the tasks they complete. Building for that future requires the right mix of specialized expertise, cross-functional relationships and technology to keep pace with social’s expanding role.

In this guide, we’ll break down how to structure a social media team, which roles to prioritize and how to build and manage a team that’s prepared for the future of marketing.

How to structure a social media team

Social’s dynamic nature can give marketers a professional advantage if leaders give them space to grow. With the right structure, teams can quickly refine and grow their skills, creating career-making opportunities.

Proactively experimenting with new social media department structures can also shift a brand’s trajectory—helping it win a larger audience, build customer loyalty and sustain growth.

Here are four common models to consider, plus how your structure may evolve as your company grows.

1. Functional

The functional model organizes social media team roles around specific responsibilities, such as influencer partnerships, social media intelligence or paid media. Generalists may also have defined focus areas, including content creation, video production and social search optimization (SOSEO).

At Sprout, the social team also partners closely with Brand Creative on asset development and with teams across the organization—including PR, Content, Customer Marketing, Events, Internal Comms, Revenue Marketing and Product Marketing—on messaging, research and distribution.

Constantly switching between incoming DMs, reporting, influencer coordination and content production can limit time for creative and strategic thinking. A functional structure can help reduce burnout, clarify ownership and create more room for social marketers to deepen their expertise.

With clearer focus areas, teams can scale priority initiatives and measure their impact more effectively. This model works especially well for organizations that want to support career development while assigning clear ownership to specific social priorities.

2. Network

Some teams align individual employees to specific networks, such as TikTok, Instagram, Facebook or LinkedIn. With this approach, each person owns a network strategy from development through execution, which in turn enables them to build deep network expertise.

Sprout’s social team experimented with a network-specific structure in 2022 before eventually moving away from it. While the model supported highly intentional content and stronger network-specific audience insights, it wasn’t scalable for a growing team.

The social landscape has also become more fluid since network-based structures first gained popularity. New networks emerge and consumer preferences change rapidly, creating gaps or redundancies when roles are tied too closely to individual networks.

A network-based social structure can still work as an interim model for lean teams developing their social media marketing strategy from the ground up. As the team grows, shifting toward functional ownership can make it easier to adapt across networks.

3. Audience engagement

Another common team structure organizes social media team roles around audience engagement goals and customer needs. These typically fall into three categories:

  • Awareness: Creating content to increase brand visibility among new and existing audiences.
  • Engagement: Creating content and responding to comments, DMs and other inbound interactions to build community and strengthen brand loyalty.
  • Customer Service: Managing customer questions, requests and complaints to resolve issues quickly.

These teams often include specialists beyond content and community management. For example, an awareness-focused team might include a content creator, an influencer marketing strategist and a performance analyst who work together to develop relevant and effective content.

Because this model requires employees to work across multiple networks, centralized social media management software becomes especially important. Bringing publishing, engagement, reporting and collaboration into one system reduces time spent switching between disconnected platforms.

4. Center of excellence

In a social media center of excellence (CoE) model, representatives from different departments form a central council that shapes social strategy and establishes shared standards.

Participants may include leaders from PR, employer brand, HR, product, customer care and other teams that rely on or contribute to social. Together, they align priorities, improve information sharing and create clearer governance around how the organization uses social.

CoE models tend to work best for large organizations with social stakeholders spread across multiple departments or regions. A centralized group reduces silos and gives distributed teams a shared framework for decision-making, measurement and execution.

5. Structure by company size

Company size can help determine which structure makes the most sense, but complexity is often the better signal. A lean team may work well with broad ownership until the volume of channels, stakeholders and social data becomes difficult for a few people to manage.

As demand grows, teams usually need more specialization and clearer ownership. Enterprise organizations also need stronger governance, especially when social intelligence spans multiple departments. articles.title: Why Reach Beats Creative: Angela Voss and Dale Harrison on the Marketing Math That Matters
articles.fullContent:
By Adweek Staff What if reaching more people matters more than creating better ads?

In this episode of Adspeak by ADWEEK, Angela Voss, CEO at Marketing Architects, and Dale Harrison, chief strategy and innovation officer at The Insight Collective, challenge conventional marketing wisdom and explore why broad, consistent reach is essential to driving market share growth.

Recorded live at Brandweek, the conversation examines why hyper-targeting can cause marketers to overlook future customers, how brands can build recall before buyers enter the market, and why overcoming the constant force of forgetting requires sustained audience reach.

Angela and Dale also explore how marketers can balance scale with cost efficiency across linear television and connected TV (CTV), using audience-first media buying and AI to cut costs.

They discuss why no single measurement model can fully capture television’s impact and how combining marketing mix modeling, attribution, and geographic holdout tests can provide a more complete picture of performance.

From smarter media allocation to long-term brand building, this episode offers practical insights into reaching more potential buyers, strengthening brand memory, and creating the conditions for sustainable growth.

Why 2x better creative can’t beat 100x greater reach

The “Surface Area of Effectiveness” framework for understanding how reach amplifies even small creative improvements

Why brand awareness only has commercial value when buyers are in-market

How to fight the constant, ongoing force of forgetting

Why hyper-targeting is “agreeing to pay more to ignore your future customers”

How to use AI-driven and audience-first media buying to cut CTV and linear TV costs

Why no single measurement model can prove TV’s value

Dale Harrison is Chief Strategy and Innovation Officer at The Insight Collective, bringing an unconventional blend of scientific rigor, technical expertise, and marketing experience. A former experimental physicist with research experience at Los Alamos and MIT, he has also worked across technology, biotech, finance, and executive management. Today, Dale combines hands-on campaign execution with a data-driven approach to marketing strategy. Drawing on his background in econometrics, mathematics, and AI, he develops rigorous experiments and sophisticated marketing models to help businesses understand what works, measure impact, and drive sustainable growth.

Angela Voss is CEO at Marketing Architects, an all-inclusive TV advertising agency specializing in linear and connected television. Drawing on her experience as a performance marketer, Angela champions greater accountability in TV advertising, making high-quality campaigns more accessible while challenging conventional approaches to audience targeting. She translates the evidence-based marketing principles of Byron Sharp and the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute into practical strategies that help brands expand their reach, build lasting brand awareness, and drive measurable growth.

articles.title: Getting Indexed No Longer Means Getting Visited via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester
articles.fullContent:
Every site owner on Google can now switch their site out of AI Overviews and AI Mode, and very few have thought about what that switch will be worth in three years. Google finished rolling the Search generative AI control out to every website worldwide on August 31, a few months after the UK Competition and Markets Authority imposed a conduct requirement obliging Google to offer exactly this kind of opt-out. The setting sits in Search Console under Settings. Google’s documentation says that once you exclude your site, its content is no longer eligible as an input to AI responses or linked from them, and that the choice is not used as a ranking signal anywhere else in Search.

Now picture the company that flips the switch. Today it looks like a contained decision, because you give up whatever AI Overviews and AI Mode send you while your organic listings stay exactly where they were. In my forecast last week , I put the window for the ranked results page to stop being Google’s default first response at 2028 to 2030, with the links one click away rather than gone. Run the opt-out forward into that window, and the company has removed itself from the surface that became the default, while keeping its place on the surface that moved behind a click. Suppose that costs another 20% of its traffic, a figure I am using to show the scale of the bet rather than one anyone has measured. Google’s position does not change either way, which is the whole point of a no-retaliation rule.

The evidence that does exist points the same direction. In Pew Research Center’s browsing analysis , users clicked a traditional result in 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% when one did not. A preregistered field experiment by researchers at Penn and Northeastern found that routing every search into AI Mode for a week cut click-through to external sites by 18.8 percentage points compared with normal Google Search. That study forced the condition, ran before AI Mode carried ads, and used participants who had rarely touched AI Mode, so it is a directional signal about a default shift rather than a forecast of one.

Here is the change underneath all of it. Being indexed used to buy a visit, and once the answer layer becomes the default, being indexed buys only eligibility, the right to be considered when a system assembles an answer, with no promise that anyone arrives at your site.

The Index Stopped Being A Shelf And Became A Candidate Pool

For more than 20 years, the bargain was easy to read. A crawler took your pages, and the search engine sent people back. Getting indexed put you on a shelf a person would scan, ranking decided how close to eye level you sat, and the visit was the payoff, with everything else happening on your own property.

In the answer layer, indexing puts you into a candidate pool , meaning the set of documents a system can draw from before it decides what to say. The system reads across that pool, selects, synthesizes, and then decides whether a link is needed at all. Google’s own wording for the new control gives the game away, because the thing you surrender by opting out is eligibility to be used as an input. That is what the index now sells. The visit has become a second event that depends on whether the answer leaves the person with a reason to keep going.

I have written before that answer engines test familiar best practices earlier in the decision chain, and that still holds for the practices themselves. What has changed is the value of the indexed state. Being in the index used to get you most of the way to a visit, and it is becoming the first of several steps, any of which can end the journey before your site sees it.

The closest precedent I know is the travel agent. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counted 61,500 travel agent jobs in 2025 and projects almost no change through 2035, and an analysis of BLS data put the drop between 2000 and 2021 at roughly 70%. The industry’s trade body has long argued that the federal count misses independent advisors, and ASTA works from a Census figure closer to 105,000 . Whichever count you prefer, the volume left once travelers could book a flight themselves, and it did not come back.

What stayed was the work the self-service channel handled badly: complicated itineraries, luxury and adventure travel, group trips, and fixing things when a connection collapses mid-journey. Host Agency Reviews’ research shows most leisure agents now run their own businesses, and that adventure and luxury specialists out-earn generalists. Their clients arrive having already done the basic research, and they are paying for judgment rather than access.

The agents who made it did not try to win the routine booking back. They rebuilt around what the new channel could not do well, priced that work properly, and accepted a smaller, more committed client base. There is a second lesson in the same BLS page, which now lists AI tools among the reasons demand may stay flat. The industry that adapted once is being asked to adapt again, and the ones best placed are those who learned the first time that the job is whatever the automated channel cannot do.

SEO does not die when the SERP stops being the default; success stops being measured by where you rank and starts being measured by whether a system selects you, which is harder to earn and harder to count. The work shifts in three ways.

The first is that content moves from capturing a query to settling a question. A page built to rank for a phrase can be summarized away in one sentence of an answer. A page that holds original data, a defined position, a clear claim with its qualifier, or an explanation nobody else has written is something a system struggles to answer well without. The test for every important page becomes whether an answer engine would produce a worse response if that page did not exist.

The second is that structure moves from keyword silos to decisions. Most sites are still organized the way crawlers and rankers rewarded, by topic and by phrase. Both the answer layer and the person who clicks through later in their thinking are better served by organization around the decisions people actually make, such as comparing options, qualifying a provider, choosing a configuration, or fixing a problem. Information architecture becomes the map that machines and people read at the same time, which is why it matters more now, not less.

The third is that the site’s job splits in two. Part of it becomes the source of record that answer engines draw from, which means consistent facts, clear entity information about who you are and what you offer, and pages that can be crawled and rendered without friction. Those are the entry fee, and they buy eligibility and nothing more. The other part becomes the conversion point for visitors who arrive having already read a synthesized answer . Those visitors skip the explainer. They want pricing, proof, comparisons, availability, and a way to reach a person. Most sites built their best real estate for the first-time visitor, and the answer layer now handles that visitor before they ever arrive.

Is The Traffic That Is Left Actually Better?

The comforting claim is that you will get less traffic but better traffic, and the evidence on that is split. Microsoft Clarity’s study of more than 1,200 publisher and news sites found AI referrals made up under 1% of traffic but converted to sign-ups at 1.66%, against 0.15% from search. A peer-reviewed paper in *Marketing Science* by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze, covering 973 ecommerce sites over twelve months, found ChatGPT referrals converted about 13% below organic search and beat only paid social, though the gap narrowed as the year went on. Different verticals, different definitions of conversion, and different time windows mean both results can be true at once.

So treat “higher quality” as a hypothesis to test on your own site, not a promise to plan around. The harder part is keeping two kinds of evidence apart. A referral session that converts is a counted number. The influence of an answer that named you without linking is an inferred one, and most dashboards blend the two without saying so. Separating them is the problem I spend most of my time on at CitationIQ, and whatever tools you use, make that separation before you base a decision on either.

The opt-out is the first time anyone has been asked to put a price on being indexed for AI features. Google’s Generative AI performance report will show you impressions from AI Overviews and AI Mode by page, country, and date, which gives you a rough view of what you would give up today. It cannot show you what you would give up in 2029, because the surface that matters most then has not become the default yet. A blanket opt-out decided on this year’s numbers prices the choice against the surface that is leaving.

Two details change the reasoning. The control does not affect AI training, which Google handles separately through Google-Extended , so anyone flipping it to protect their content from model training gets neither the protection nor the traffic. And the CMA’s deadline for page-level controls falls in March 2027, which turns an all-or-nothing choice into a page-by-page one. Protecting a proprietary research page while leaving in the pages whose job is to be selected is a defensible use of that control. Pulling the whole site out of the surface your future customers will start on is a harder case to make.

The forecast range gives most businesses two to four years, and the slowest work is exactly what cannot be rushed in 2029. Rebuilding content around questions you can settle, reorganizing a site around decisions, and retooling measurement so counted and inferred numbers stay separate all take longer than a redesign cycle. Start with the pages that carry the most commercial weight and ask, honestly, whether a system could answer the buyer’s question just as well without them. If it could, that page has no reason to be selected, and no ranking will save it.

When the ranked list stops being the default, being indexed buys eligibility rather than a visit, and the businesses that keep earning from search will be the ones whose content a system cannot answer well without.

If you have already flipped the toggle, or decided not to, tell me how you decided that in the comments, because I would like to see the reasoning people are using.

Welcome back to AI, Tech & Money. This is Trishla Ostwal, ADWEEK’s AI reporter, back in New York City after a week in London, where I moderated a panel at Semrush Spotlight. I also watched OpenAI make the case that the most effective method to sell ChatGPT to businesses in Europe is the old-fashioned way: in person, at events. 

Online, OpenAI is moving a lot faster. It said Wednesday that over 100,000 advertisers have now run campaigns on ChatGPT, and it’s expanding ChatGPT Ads into 26 more countries. 

But most of my week went to Meta, which has been in the ads game nearly two decades longer than OpenAI. I read its new business terms more times than I’d like to admit, and the short version is this: from Oct. 30, if Meta’s AI messes up your ad, that’s on you. Buyers I spoke with said Meta’s AI is already reworking their ads without asking. More on that in a minute. 

The new terms land in a busy week for Meta. A New Mexico judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found in September that Facebook misled users about how much control they had over their data. Meta is expected to appeal. The same day, Meta also reported $64.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, beating Wall Street’s estimate of about $63.3 billion.

OpenAI wants a bigger number on the board, too. It’s in talks to raise about $30 billion at a valuation above $1.4 trillion, according to Reuters, up from the $852 billion it hit in March after a record $122 billion round. 

The timing is the tell. OpenAI wants to price the round before Anthropic’s expected mid-November IPO, when Anthropic’s disclosures will let investors compare the two businesses side by side. 

Anthropic’s own number has been sliding: Investors at its Oct. 14 investor day discussed a valuation around $1.5 trillion, down from the roughly $2 trillion it had sought, after third-quarter growth slowed. 

From January to July, news sites made up an average of 29.5% of ChatGPT’s cited sources in the U.K., according to Semrush’s AI Visibility Index shared with me; in the U.S., the number fell to 19.6%. ChatGPT had the highest news share of the four AI platforms each month, in both markets, ahead of Google’s Gemini, AI overviews and AI mode. Moreover, every platform leaned more heavily on news in the U.K. 

ChatGPT isn’t necessarily favoring news sites by design, according to  Semrush. I sat down with Eli Goodman, Semrush’s svp, product solutions, at its  Spotlight event. He said the difference in citations across both the markets is tied to how people in each market consume news. In the U.S., news content is more blended with opinion, and trust in the media has fallen over the past decade or more compared with the U.K., he said. 

People in the U.K. consume more news, Goodman added, and because LLMs try to reason like humans, they end up mirroring that behavior. With news accounting for close to 30% of ChatGPT’s U.K. citations, Goodman said, PR has become an important part of how brands are viewed as sources.

Meta’s AI has been editing advertisers’ ads on its platforms. 

Bookshop.org, the online bookseller, found out the hard way. In a post on Threads, the bookseller said that an automated account update from Meta opted it into a generative AI feature, which added an AI-generated illustration to its human-made ad without its knowledge.

“This particular ad was ‘enhanced’ (or ruined, really) by Meta without our knowledge after an account update opted us in to their new ad features last week,” the company wrote on Threads. It has since turned off all of Meta’s AI ad features.

Advertisers have had their issues with Meta’s AI features for a long time. What appears to be more recent developments are Meta’s AI making enhancements without being asked, and the liability for any inaccuracies landing on the advertiser.

“As we saw with Bookshop, these automatic genAI revisions can be antithetical to brands’ strategies and their values, and [can] publish without a brand even knowing it,” said Emarketer’s senior analyst Asa Hiken. “It’s the brand that stands to lose here; consumers are unaware of Meta’s ad policies and are thus likely to assume that the brand willingly used AI.”

Digital agency Exverus told me Meta’s AI is tacking on sitelinks, translating copy, and spinning up AI images and carousels out of a brand’s own photos, sometimes on ads where advertisers did not switch the feature on. 

Starting Oct. 30, all that is legally the advertiser’s problem. Under Meta’s updated Commercial Terms, the contract that governs every business using its products, advertisers who run ads on Meta will be “solely responsible” for whatever its AI features create or change, including features Meta switches on. This language sits in a new section, ‘AI Features,’ that does not exist in the current version. 

Previously, according to the terms, liability stood with advertisers as well but only if they chose to use Meta’s AI tools. 

“You may choose to use the Ad Creative AIs in your sole discretion and that your use of the Ad Creative AIs may result in Output that is digitally created, enhanced or altered and that such Output may be inaccurate, incomplete, misleading, offensive, and/or inappropriate,” the terms read. “You also recognize and agree that you–not Meta–are responsible for your use of any Output, and/or any actions you take in relation to your Ad Content.”

articles.title: Why Reddit Belongs In Your PR Strategy via @sejournal, @brentcsutoras
articles.fullContent:
I remember the first time I saw national news networks using Twitter as a source of news and checking in with people to hear what they thought. To me, that was a moment when social media became mainstream and started to feel normal for the wider public.

Having been on Reddit for 20 years, I’ve seen a lot of its content show up elsewhere, so that isn’t new to me. There are Tom’s Guide articles built around Reddit recommendations, Smosh shows about Reddit stories, and films like Dumb Money , but over the last year, I’ve been seeing more and more examples.

A recommendation that comes from Reddit feels different from a collection of reviews on a website . People show the value they place in those conversations through what they read, click on, and recommend. That doesn’t make every account authentic or every opinion representative, but it explains why the source itself has become part of the selling point.

A few months back, I saw a Newsweek article about a Reddit post claiming a local Panera had removed almost all its power outlets. The post had become the source of the story.

The April 1, 2026 post included a photo and described a cafe near a university where outlets had been replaced with blanking plates, leaving people unable to plug in a phone or laptop.

Two days later, Newsweek covered the complaint , embedding the post and reactions from the discussion. The reporter contacted the poster and Panera, but said it couldn’t verify the details. The complaint concerned one cafe and didn’t confirm a company-wide policy.

Around that same time, I noticed an Allrecipes article showing up through Yahoo about Panera’s Sip Club changes. Published in July, it also referenced Reddit. The policy details came from Panera’s FAQ, while the Reddit discussion showed how people felt about the change.

These were two stories I’d come across back-to-back where Reddit was making pretty decent news. It reminded me of just how valuable Reddit is beyond the platform itself.

A Temu Purchase Became A Technology Story

On May 2, Tom’s Hardware reported on a Reddit user’s account of buying a purported 4TB external drive on Temu for $20. Their teardown photos showed a microSD card reader glued inside the enclosure. The article embedded the post and later added a response from a Temu spokesperson.

A Restaurant Dispute Reached The Local News

On May 22, Boston.com covered a dispute involving Olivia’s Kitchen in Somerville . Screenshots of a review and a sharply worded restaurant reply had been shared in r/Somerville. The review started elsewhere, but Reddit was where the screenshots and discussion surfaced for this coverage.

The reporter obtained a statement from the owner, who said the reply hadn’t been authorized and tap water would be served on request starting that week. That sequence doesn’t establish that Reddit alone caused the policy change.

A Micro Center Purchase Form Became A Story

On October 2, PC Gamer covered a buyer’s Reddit post about a declaration required when purchasing an RTX 5090-equipped computer at Micro Center’s Tustin store. The buyer shared the form and described the requirement, giving the publication a document and a first-person account to report on.

Tom’s Hardware and TechRadar also covered the incident. Those articles represent further coverage of the same post, and the account doesn’t establish a requirement at every store.

There’s definitely value in connecting with people on Reddit and in the way those conversations can appear in search and AI answers . Pew’s 2025 survey found that 26% of U.S. adults reported ever using Reddit. The Panera examples show that those conversations can also reach people through news coverage.

In a 2023 survey of 629 U.S. health journalists , 20.3% reported using Reddit to find story ideas. The possibility of a conversation becoming a news story makes it more imperative for brands to be part of the conversation and present on Reddit.

If you’re present on Reddit and have a good community, I think people are more likely to bring problems to you. Your own subreddit gives that community a place to help resolve them with you, giving you a chance to address issues before they spread into other subreddits or the news.

There’s also a reason to pay attention along the user journey . In a 2024 GWI study conducted with Reddit across the U.S., UK, and Germany, 69% of surveyed people using Reddit for product research said they were seeking other people’s opinions or experiences.

I see a real disconnect between what brands think people will talk about and what they actually talk about. Most of our work these days is helping brands understand the user journey and figure out where they’re a good fit to answer a question, solve a problem, or help someone make a decision.

That’s valuable for marketing, social media, search, PR, customer support, product development, and the executive team. I would connect those teams so a product problem, a support need, or a possible news story reaches someone who can give a useful answer.

I would make the affiliation clear, follow each community’s rules , and help where the brand has something useful to offer. Being present gives the team a chance to address problems, but it doesn’t put the brand in control of every conversation or the coverage that follows.

See also: AMA: Reddit Marketing Veteran Shares What Works On The Platform

I would track whether a conversation was used in a news article, what the reporter took from it, and whether the brand’s response appeared. If a story links to the site, look at its referral traffic and what those visitors do. Track original reporting separately from syndicated copies, and read the coverage before deciding what it means for the business.

These examples don’t tell us how often a Reddit post will receive coverage or prove that the frequency is increasing. The practice has been around for years, including earlier reporting built around Reddit accounts .

When I think about Reddit’s value, I would include news coverage alongside the community relationships, search visibility , and AI discovery we’re already talking about.

articles.title: Week of Oct. 5 Morning News Ratings: CBS Mornings Grows
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro CBS News’ CBS Mornings finished the week of October 5 as the only morning show to record gains in both total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo. NBC News’s Today joined CBS News’ morning show in registering gains in the advertiser-coveted demo.

Today widened the gap over ABC News’ Good Morning America to more than 170,000 viewers. This comes as GMA, the only broadcast to lose viewers in both measurements, shrank the demo gap the previous week to exactly 100,000 viewers.

According to Nielsen’s national live+same-day big data plus program ratings, GMA averaged 2.683 million total viewers and 467,000 viewers in the A25-54 demo for the week of Oct. 5. Compared to the previous week , ABC News’ morning show dropped by -1% in total viewers and -4% in the demo—the only broadcast to lose viewers in both measurements. When looking at how it performed in the same week in 2025, GMA was down -4% in total viewers and -6% in the demo.

Today remained in first place in total viewers and the demo, with 2.859 million and 640,000 viewers, respectively, for the week that just ended. Today was flat in total viewers and up +9% in the A25-54 demo compared to the previous week. When put up against the same week in 2025 , Today was up +9% in total viewers and +13% in the demo.

CBS Mornings had 1.735 million total viewers and 294,000 viewers in the demo for the week of Oct. 5. Compared with the previous week, CBS News’ morning show grew by +1% in total viewers and +7% in the demo—the only morning show with gains in either of the measured categories. Versus the same week in 2025, CBS Mornings was down -8% in total viewers and -2% in the demo.

  1. The most important employee advocacy metrics tie directly to business outcomes: reach, engagement, leads, hires, and ad spend saved.
  2. Calculating employee advocacy ROI means assigning dollar values to revenue, recruiting savings, paid media savings, and retention savings, then comparing that total against program costs.

What does it mean to measure employee advocacy success?

Measuring employee advocacy success means evaluating your program’s business impact through key performance indicators (KPIs). A complete measurement approach tracks:

  • Reach and brand visibility: How far employee posts extend your brand beyond corporate channels
  • Engagement: Whether audiences are interacting with employee-shared content
  • Employee participation: How many employees are actively sharing, and how often
  • Business impact: This includes leads, conversions, hires, and ad spend saved

Tracking results turns fluffy numbers into evidence you can take to leadership. And with the right data, you can sharpen your strategy into a repeatable advocacy machine.

Real-world example: Victoria Samways, Marketing & Brand Manager at Major Tom, used employee advocacy measurement to prove a three-figure ROI on a single campaign.

  • The approach: Samways paired employee advocacy software with UTM tracking codes, then encouraged employees to share campaign content.
  • The result: Advocacy landed in Major Tom’s top 5 traffic sources for the campaign, generated over $100k in pipeline, and delivered a higher-than-average win rate.

“Thanks to the UTM tracking links, over the coming weeks, we saw a healthy amount of leads that we attributed back to this campaign,” Samways shares. “This resulted in over $100k in our pipeline and, as a channel, provided a higher-than-average win rate due to the referral-like context of these leads.”

Why is it important to measure employee advocacy success?

Measurement matters because advocacy programs compete for budget, attention, and headcount like every other initiative. Without data, they almost always lose that competition.

Here are three specific risks of running an unmeasured employee advocacy program:

  1. You can’t defend your budget. Measurement shows how your program moves the needle on reach, leads, and recruiting.
  2. You can’t fix what’s broken. Without data, you don’t know if low participation is a content problem, a platform problem, or a culture problem.
  3. You can’t replicate what’s working. Measurement shows you which campaigns, content types, and brand advocates are driving the strongest results. When you know what’s working, you can streamline your efforts and scale the wins.

There’s another upside that’s easy to underestimate: measurement makes employees take the program more seriously. And with 2026 social trends pointing to ROI as the defining factor of ambassador programs, that rigor has never been more important.

When employee advocates can see their own impact, they participate more and stick with the program longer. In other words, the act of measuring is itself a participation lever.

The bottom line: A social media post that racks up a thousand likes feels great, but if those likes aren’t turning into top talent, qualified leads, or customers, what’s the point? Measurement is what makes the impact of employee advocacy visible.

Source: Balaji Mohanty

How do you build an employee advocacy measurement framework?

You build an employee advocacy measurement framework by deciding what the program is meant to achieve, then choosing the employee advocacy KPIs that map to each goal. Doing this first saves you from drowning in metrics that nobody in the business cares about.

Here’s a simple four-step framework to work through before you track a single share:

  1. Define your goals: Pick one or two primary outcomes, such as brand awareness, lead generation, recruiting, or retention. Most programs try to serve all four at once and end up proving none of them.
  2. Map metrics to each goal: Awareness goals need reach and impressions. Lead-gen goals need clicks, conversions, and pipeline influence. Recruiting goals need applicant volume and time-to-hire.
  3. Set your baselines: Record where each metric sits before the program launches (or before your next big push). Without a baseline, you have numbers but no story.
  4. Agree on a reporting cadence: Review participation and engagement monthly so you can course-correct quickly. Save business impact metrics like pipeline and earned media value for quarterly reviews.

What is social media in healthcare?

Social media in healthcare is the use of public social platforms by healthcare organizations to communicate with patients, educate the public, recruit staff, and build their brand. That includes hospitals and health systems, private clinics and group practices, public health agencies, pharmaceutical and medical device companies, and individual clinicians posting in a professional capacity.

In practice, most healthcare social media activity falls into a handful of use cases:

  • Patient engagement: Answering common questions, sharing service updates, and staying connected between visits.
  • Health education: Explaining conditions, procedures, and preventive care in plain language.
  • Recruitment and employer branding: Showing what it’s like to work at your organization.
  • Brand building: Establishing credibility and patient trust before someone becomes a patient.
  • Crisis communication: Responding quickly to incidents, closures, or negative press.
  • Public health outreach: Promoting screenings, vaccination campaigns, and community programs.

What makes healthcare different from other industries is the regulation. Marketing teams in most sectors worry about tone and timing. For those in the B2B health space, social media is both a way to promote your products to healthcare organizations and help contribute to public health literacy with educational content.

articles.title: 11 employee advocacy program examples for 2026
articles.fullContent:
What is an employee advocacy program?

An employee advocacy program is a structured initiative that encourages employees to share company-approved content on their personal social media accounts to extend brand reach and build trust.

It’s a powerful part of any social media marketing and content strategy. Instead of relying only on your brand’s accounts to do the talking, employees post about your company on platforms like LinkedIn, X, or wherever they’re already active.

Sometimes that content is promotional, like a new campaign, product launch, or company milestone. Other times it’s cultural, offering a peek into what it’s actually like to work at your company.

The reason it works is simple: people trust other people more than they trust corporations. In fact, 88% of consumers say trusting a brand is an important or critical purchase criterion, on par with quality and value, according to Edelman.

When your employees share authentic stories, it humanizes your brand, boosts your organic reach, and helps you connect with your target audience in ways standard corporate messaging just can’t.

Successful employee advocacy programs are built on:

  • Clear marketing goals
  • Measurable KPIs to track performance
  • Easy-to-share content and guidelines for employees

The benefits for the company are wide-reaching:

  • Increased brand awareness,
  • Improved reputation,
  • Boosted engagement, and
  • Talent recruitment, to name a few.

In short, every employee share strengthens both your internal company culture and your external trust, turning your team into your most credible marketing channel.

Download a free employee advocacy toolkit that shows you how to plan, launch, and grow a successful employee advocacy program for your organization.

Download now

Informal advocacy vs. structured programs: what’s the difference?

The difference between informal advocacy and a structured program comes down to intention.

  • Informal advocacy: Spontaneous and personal. Genuine, but unpredictable. You can’t count on it, measure it, or repeat it.
  • Structured programs: Intentional, consistent, and built to scale, because employees get the tools, content, and guidelines they need to share regularly.

Most successful employee advocacy programs include:

  • Curated content hubs: Where employees can access pre-approved content
  • Training and resources: To help staff build their personal brand while staying on-message
  • Incentives or recognition: That encourage ongoing participation
  • Measurement and analytics: To track reach, engagement, and business impact

A platform like Parliament, the employee advocacy app inside Hootsuite Social OS, makes this simple. Employees get a curated feed of pre-approved content they can post in a few taps, while admins measure performance across every share, gamify participation with leaderboards, and keep posts aligned with brand and legal guidelines.

Summary: Informal advocacy is spontaneous and personal. Structured programs are intentional and strategic.

Why do companies invest in employee advocacy programs?

Companies invest in employee advocacy programs because they drive real business outcomes: wider reach, stronger reputation, better recruitment, and more pipeline, all at a fraction of the cost of traditional marketing.

To understand what this looks like in practice, we chatted with Victoria Samways, Marketing & Brand Manager at Major Tom, and a long-time user of Hootsuite’s employee advocacy tools.

“Our employees are very powerful brand ambassadors,” says Samways. “Each employee can easily have hundreds of connections on LinkedIn alone. Multiply that by the number of employees a brand has, and that’s a large audience.“

Here are the top employee advocacy benefits:

  1. Expanded brand reach and awareness
  2. Stronger talent attraction and recruiting
  3. Improved brand reputation and trust
  4. Higher organic engagement
  5. Sales pipeline and lead generation
  6. Career and personal brand benefits for employees

1. Expanded brand reach and awareness

Collectively, employees have a wide social reach. Tapping into your employees’ networks is one of the easiest ways to reach new audiences without spending a dollar on paid media. And it also feels more authentic.

The math is straightforward. A company of 500 employees with 500 LinkedIn connections each has access to a potential audience of 250,000 people, most of whom will never follow the brand page. That’s why brand reach is usually the first metric advocacy programs move.

2. Stronger talent attraction and recruiting

A careers page can promise great culture all day long, but a real employee sharing what it’s actually like to work there? That’s way more convincing.

When teams post authentically about their work (wins, projects, team moments, or even just what a typical day looks like), it offers a genuine peek at the employee experience.

articles.fullContent:
Black Friday prep is happening earlier than ever for shoppers this year. Your customers are already looking for deals online and increasingly on social media. According to a Q3 2026 Sprout Social Pulse Survey, 78% of users plan to use social as much or more than they did last year to help them find and purchase gifts this year.

Social media is now tied with physical stores for gift purchase discovery, with 46% of customers marking them as top choices. As customers face increasing economic pressure this year, many are using social media to research the best deals. If you want to make the most of Black Friday on social media, start planning your strategy now. Customers are eager for ideas well before November.

In this guide, we walk through how to build effective Black Friday social media campaigns this Q4.

5 types of Black Friday social media posts (+ examples)

Spurred by the growth of online shopping and social commerce, Black Friday has become a multi-day event, including Small Business Saturday and Cyber Monday. According to the data, customers are thinking about their holiday shopping differently this year, and ecommerce is a key part of their plans.

More than half of respondents (69%) to the Q3 2026 pulse survey said they’re concerned about rising prices due to tariffs. Over a third (36%) are planning to shop earlier to specifically avoid tariff-related price jumps, and 56% are planning to reduce their holiday spending overall due to economic conditions.

For brands, that means competition is higher and earning customer trust will take more legwork. To create a winning Black Friday marketing strategy, it’s crucial to tap into the power of social.

Nearly a quarter (23%) of the Q3 pulse survey respondents said the quality of a company’s social media customer service makes them more likely to purchase this holiday season, and a similar percentage said the originality of holiday-specific social content makes a difference. Here are different types of Black Friday social media posts that have worked for other brands to inspire your campaign planning.

Influencer collaborations

Partner with influencers to create tailored content for specific demographics. From fashion lovers to tech enthusiasts, influencers can connect with high-intent niche audiences. If your Black Friday deals are perfect for a particular type of customer, working with influencers who already speak to that crowd can build trust and revenue

Offering special discounts and promo codes via influencers is one way to track ROI of a campaign and boost sales. In fact, promo codes are the leading factor influencing the purchasing decisions of social media scrollers. Thirty percent of respondents to the Q3 pulse survey said promo codes influencers share make them more likely to purchase from a brand during the holidays, more than any other factor in the survey.

Keep in mind that follower count is not the main barometer of impact for your influencer partnerships. Instead, focus on social media discoverability. Working with influencers who can create hyper-relevant content is key to getting your campaign seen by new audiences. Small businesses with modest budgets and larger companies alike can embrace micro-influencer marketing this gifting season.

For example, Rilee Smith, a travel and packing influencer on Instagram, crafted a video in partnership with five of her favorite bag brands to offer her followers a slate of Black Friday sales. Her video showed each of the bags in action and what discounts the brands offered.

What is social media analytics?

  • Diagnostic: Why did it happen? (e.g., posting frequency decreased during a team transition)
  • Predictive: What’s likely to happen next? (e.g., engagement will rebound if posting cadence returns to normal)

That shift has important implications for content teams, particularly as AI changes how audiences discover and evaluate information.

The opportunity isn’t simply to produce more content with AI. Brands need systems that connect audience insights, human expertise, content creation, distribution, and performance measurement. articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Websites remain an important way for consumers to verify that a business is legitimate.
  • Wix’s State of Websites report found that search still accounts for 42% of website traffic.
  • Sites with structured data that passes Google’s rich-results inspection earn 2x more revenue and 9x more traffic than sites without it.
  • Blogs and reviews can strengthen a brand’s authority and contribute to business growth.
  • As AI changes discovery, a credible website can give consumers and AI systems a reliable source of information about a brand.

AI has made it easier than ever to create a website, generate content, and put a brand online. That speed comes with a new challenge: consumers have more reason to question what they see.

A convincing business can appear online almost overnight. For customers, a website therefore has an important job beyond selling products or services. It can help establish that a business is real.

Wix’s first State of Websites report, based on data from more than 300 million users, examines how websites are being built, discovered, and used in the age of AI. The report found that websites remain central to business growth, even as discovery expands across AI platforms and other channels.

For marketers, the takeaway is straightforward. Website credibility still matters. The challenge is making sure a website provides the information, content, and technical signals that support trust with both people and machines.

Why Websites Still Matter in the Age of AI

AI search is changing how people find information, but it hasn’t eliminated the need for a destination where customers can verify what they’ve learned.

Source

Websites Help Consumers Verify a Business

Wix’s research describes a growing tension around AI and website creation. Building a site is becoming faster, but customers still need confidence that a business is legitimate.

A consumer might discover a company through an AI recommendation, social platform, or traditional search result. Before making a purchase or contacting the business, they may visit its website to confirm that the company exists and learn more about what it offers.

That makes a website part of the validation process.

A professional domain, clear business information, useful content, customer reviews, and evidence of expertise can all contribute to website trust. These signals help answer a basic question that becomes increasingly important as AI-generated information becomes easier to produce: Is this business real?

AI Search Is Changing Discovery, Not Replacing Websites

The Wix report found that AI platforms are increasingly interacting with websites. Its data shows that LLMs still account for less than 1% of website traffic, although traffic from LLMs grew fourfold between 2024 and 2025.

Traditional search remains much more significant. Search accounts for 42% of traffic to Wix sites, compared with 40% from direct traffic and 13% from social.

This puts the current state of discovery into perspective. AI search is growing quickly, but traditional search continues to be a major source of website visits.

For brands, that means the website still needs to serve both audiences: people arriving directly or through search and AI systems looking for information to use in their responses.

What the Wix Data Says About Website Trust

The report highlights several website characteristics associated with stronger business performance.


Source

Structured Data Can Support Visibility

One of the clearest findings concerns structured data.

Wix found that sites with structured data markup that passed Google’s rich-results inspection earned 2x more revenue and received 9x more traffic than sites without it.

This is a correlation in Wix’s dataset, not evidence that adding structured data directly causes those outcomes. Still, the finding reinforces the importance of making website information easier for search engines and AI systems to understand.

Structured data gives machines additional context about the information presented on a page. As search experiences become more sophisticated, that machine-readable layer can help make important information easier to interpret.

For brands investing in AI visibility, technical foundations such as structured data should therefore remain part of the conversation.

articles.title: Building trust through social media: 5 ways to earn it
articles.fullContent:
Authenticity is the most important brand characteristic on social media, according to Sprout’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey. But as audiences grow more skeptical of what they see in their feeds, brands need to work harder to earn their trust.

People rely on social media for news, product recommendations and connection. At the same time, Sprout’s Q1 2026 Pulse Survey found that 35% of users trust social media less than they did a year ago. AI-generated content adds to that skepticism, making it harder to distinguish real experiences from manufactured ones.

Sprout’s Be So FR webinar explored this “trust recession” and the growing demand for content that reflects real people and experiences. Brands need to show who’s behind their content and follow through when customers reach out.

Building trust through social media starts with what you publish and how you respond to your audience. In this guide, we’ll explore what earns audience trust and practical ways to strengthen it.

Why trust is now built on social media first

People often encounter your brand through someone else’s post before they visit your website. They search for recommendations, compare customer experiences and ask questions in the comments. Those interactions help them decide whether to trust you.

Sprout’s 2026 Pulse Surveys show how people use social to find information and decide what to buy:

  • Search: 21% of consumers turn to social media first when searching for information, according to Q2 data.
  • Influencer impact: 67% made a purchase directly because of an influencer’s recommendation in the past year.
  • Trends and culture: Q3 data found that 54% of consumers turn to social media to keep up with trends and cultural moments, ahead of TV and streaming at 45% and conversations with friends and family at 42%.

These social media statistics show why brands need to pay attention to conversations beyond their own accounts. With influencers playing such a significant role in what people buy, choosing credible partners matters.

For example, viewers of @theglownarrative’s skincare review discuss product prices, share what they want to try and recommend alternatives. Her review gives viewers a starting point, while the comments offer additional perspectives. Brands that partner with creators who share honest, firsthand experiences give potential customers more reason to trust their products.


The same online scrutiny applies when something goes wrong for a brand too. According to Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, consumers first hear about a brand crisis on social. And 64% say it’s important for brands to respond publicly on social rather than through a press release or website statement.

How building trust on social media is a growth lever

Social media’s influence gives brands a chance to turn audience trust into growth. When people trust your brand, they’re more likely to choose your products and recommend them to others. As Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey highlights, creating multiple points of connection with your brand and through partnerships with trusted voices can strengthen customer relationships and support growth:

  • Authentic influencer partnerships build buying confidence. Eighty-one percent of consumers say it matters whether an influencer has used the product they promote. Creators with firsthand product experience offer more credible recommendations.
  • Employee content introduces potential customers to your business. Forty percent of consumers rated employee-generated content as more authentic than posts from a brand’s main account. The same proportion discover products or services through employee content at least once a month.
  • Timely crisis responses protect customer relationships. Response speed influences how consumers judge a brand’s public crisis response. Addressing problems promptly and following through on a solution gives customers a reason to keep doing business with you.

The signals that earn audience trust

Building audience confidence starts with how your brand shows up day to day. The table below outlines four trust builders—consistency, responsiveness, transparency and proof—and the behaviors that undermine them.

Trust builder Trust breaker Consistency: Maintain a recognizable voice and follow through on your stated values. Chase trends that clash with your identity or make promises your actions don’t support. Responsiveness: Acknowledge questions promptly and provide helpful answers or clear next steps. Ignore customer concerns or send generic replies that don’t address the issue. Transparency: Disclose relevant AI use and paid partnerships, and acknowledge mistakes. Hide sponsorships, present AI-generated content as real experiences or avoid accountability. Proof: Share customer experiences, employee expertise and recommendations from creators who know your products. Rely on unsupported claims or endorsements from people with no firsthand product experience.

Consistency

A consistent voice and posting cadence set expectations for your brand. Your values need the same follow-through: if you promote a commitment to customer care, your replies should reflect it. Maintain that reliability across everyday posts, campaigns and difficult conversations.

Responsiveness

Helpful replies show customers that you take their concerns seriously. Sprout’s Q3 pulse survey found that 38% expect a customer care response within two hours, including 14% who expect one within minutes.

For example, SpotifyCares responds to a creator’s upload problem within minutes, connects them with the right team and invites them to follow up if they run into issues.


Speed matters during crises, too, as Q2 pulse survey findings show. Acknowledge the issue promptly, explain what you know and tell people when to expect an update. The quality of your response matters as much as how quickly you send it.

Transparency

Be up front about how you create your content and what you’re promoting. That includes paid partnerships, relevant AI use and the limits of your product claims.

Sprout’s Q1 pulse survey found that 28% of consumers most want brands to stop posting AI-generated content without labels. Disclose when content is AI-generated and have a person check it for accuracy before publishing. Disclosure explains how you created it, while human review reduces the risk of publishing inaccurate information.

articles.title: Personal branding: What it is and how to build yours
articles.fullContent:
You’ve heard it from mentors, recruiters and that coworker who posts on LinkedIn every morning: You need a personal brand. Truth is, you already have one, because people form a public perception of your brand whether you shape it or not. This guide shows you how to take control of that perception and turn it into real opportunities.

Personal branding once sounded like a celebrity-only game. Today, founders, marketers, job seekers and employees use it to stand out in crowded feeds and earn trust before they ever say hello. It’s how people decide whether to follow you, hire you or buy from you.

Branding yourself feels daunting when you don’t know where to start. But the strongest personal brands are built on who you already are.

You don’t need a massive following, a big budget or a magnetic personality. You need well-defined goals, a sharp sense of your value and the habit of showing up.

Ready to build yours? Let’s dig in.

What is personal branding?

Personal branding is how you present yourself as an individual to your audience. It’s the mix of expertise, values and personality people associate with your name. Our glossary definition covers the short version, and this guide shows you how to build one.

The idea isn’t new. Management writer Tom Peters popularized it in 1997 with his Fast Company essay “The Brand Called You.” Social media turned his idea into something anyone with a phone can act on.

Think about how corporate branding works. We associate specific feelings, values and expectations with brands we trust. Every company has a story and image.

The same applies to you and your personal brand. The difference comes down to who owns it, how it sounds and what it’s for.

People often treat personal branding as a synonym for being an influencer. It doesn’t have to be. A software engineer, a nurse and a small business owner can each build a personal brand without chasing fame.

Your brand should highlight your human side. Voices and personalities set brands (and people!) apart. Branding yourself means aligning your online persona with your real-life one.

Building your brand goes beyond just marketing yourself. Here are the key pieces of a personal brand:

  • Voice and values. That is, what you say and what you believe. Your brand voice shouldn’t be one-size-fits-all or robotic.

  • Content. What you create, and how you present it, attracts your audience. If you write long-form newsletters, mastering Substack SEO gets those deep dives discovered by new readers.

  • Creativity. You don’t need to be a creative genius to build a personal brand. But some sort of creative trademark helps you stand out from the crowd.

  • Personality. There’s no one-size-fits-all personality type for your brand. Energetic, laid back or suit-and-tie, you do you.

  • Authenticity. Your personal brand shouldn’t feel manufactured or made up. Align your online persona with who you are offline and your brand will never feel forced.

Why is personal branding important?

Here is why building a personal brand is worth the effort.

Standing out from the crowd

The people who’d benefit the most from a personal brand are often focused on building something else. A company, art, you name it.

Like it or not, everyone’s a content creator now. That means who we are and what we make are often one and the same.

Among the countless creators and marketers out there, growth is daunting. Your audience only has so much attention to give.

With a compelling brand and consistent content, you give yourself a chance to shine. People don’t grow audiences or garner influence by accident. And both your personal brand and what you create sit within your control.

Relatability and authenticity matter to modern audiences

According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, consumers rank authenticity and relatability as two of the three most important brand content traits. Apply the same logic to individuals. This matters even more in an era where “influence” can feel manufactured.

That’s your edge as an individual. Nobody else has your experiences, your opinions or your sense of humor.

Making stronger connections with your community

Your voice and values shape your ability to grow your audience. Putting your personality front and center attracts like-minded followers.

That also means engaging with your audience to understand their needs and challenges. This goes hand in hand with establishing trust and building meaningful relationships.

When followers feel seen, they comment, share and come back for more. That’s how an audience becomes a community.

Opening doors to career and business opportunities

A strong personal brand puts your expertise on display before anyone asks for it. Recruiters, clients, collaborators and event organizers find you, instead of the other way around.

The 2025 Edelman-LinkedIn B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report found that thought leadership builds trust and opens doors where ads and traditional sales methods fall short. When you share your expertise in your own voice, you become the kind of thought leader buyers want to hear from.

What makes a strong personal brand?

A strong personal brand is specific, consistent and rooted in real value. Before you post anything, get well-defined answers to these questions.

  • Purpose: Why you’re building a brand at all (a new role, clients, a community or a product launch).

  • Niche: The narrow topic you want to be known for. Precision is memorable and breadth is forgettable.

  • Audience: The specific people you want to reach and the problems they need solved.

  • Value: What you give that audience that no one else does (expertise, perspective, entertainment or community).

  • Story: The experiences that explain why you care and why people should listen to you.

articles.title: How Atlas Copco Group built a proactive reputation intelligence model
articles.fullContent:
Reputation risk often shows up in small ways first. Customer concerns in one market, inconsistent messaging in another. Different teams respond to the same issue in different ways. Individually, they may seem minor. Together, they can reveal a much bigger problem.

Part of the challenge is how brands track reputation risk in the first place. Traditional approaches often focus on obvious changes after they happen, rather than connecting social and media signals that could point to an issue sooner. As a result, teams can miss early warning signs or struggle to piece them together quickly enough.

Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report found that most teams take one to two weeks to act on what they see on social, while only 10% respond within hours. This delay has real consequences. Eighty-six percent of organizations say siloed or slow-moving insights have caused them to miss opportunities, and 26% have seen customer issues escalate that could have been addressed earlier.

Atlas Copco Group, a global industrial company spanning air compression, vacuum, industrial and power technologies, wanted better visibility into those warning signs. Their approach shows what it looks like to move beyond monitoring and use reputation data more proactively. This article breaks down their process to show what a stronger reputation intelligence model looks like in practice.

What is reputation intelligence? (And why monitoring no longer cuts it)

Reputation intelligence connects brand data across markets, channels and social accounts so teams can spot patterns, understand them and decide what needs attention.

Reputation monitoring, on the other hand, focuses on tracking what’s already happening around your brand. It tracks signals like reviews, mentions and shifts in sentiment. Monitoring helps teams keep tabs on public perception, while reputation intelligence adds the context needed to make more proactive decisions.

For large organizations, that broader view turns scattered brand feedback into clearer guidance for communications, go-to-market strategies, governance and other business decisions. Teams can use the same reputation data to identify recurring issues and give leaders a better view of developing risks in the business.

Reputation risk hides in small signals, not big spikes

Many reputation management services focus on obvious changes, like a sudden spike in negative sentiment or a surge in brand mentions. By then, the issue is already visible enough to demand a response or have caused damage.

The first clues are usually less obvious. Maybe your customers start complaining about the same thing or more of their questions go unanswered. Engagement might drop or online conversations about your brand might take on a more negative tone.

When Atlas Copco Group’s team dug into how conversations about their brand actually evolved, they saw that many risks started as smaller patterns: repeated questions, inconsistent account activity, off-brand content, inactive pages, declining quality signals or fragmented local execution.

These signals are easy to miss when you rely on alerts alone because each one can seem too minor to warrant attention. With social intelligence, Atlas Copco Group brings those signals together to spot patterns that need a closer look before they impact business performance.

Atlas Copco Group’s 5-step reputation intelligence model

Atlas Copco Group manages social in multiple business areas, divisions and local markets. Operating at this scale means protecting brand trust and compliance while enabling local teams to respond quickly to their audiences.

The team addressed that challenge by shifting from reactive reputation management to a more proactive governance model, earning Atlas Copco Group Sprout’s 2026 Predictive Edge Award.

The model is based on five practices that help them spot emerging risk, strengthen brand presence and manage issues consistently.

1. Catch weak signals early

Atlas Copco Group tracks weak signals that could point to larger reputation issues. Recurring customer and internal team behavior patterns are all indicators that brand consistency or account health may be slipping. Tracking these patterns across markets helps the global team focus on the bigger picture and provide guidance so local teams can stay close to their audiences and market.

To identify which weak signals matter for your brand, start with the reputation risks you already monitor and work backward. What behaviors, questions or changes tend to show up before those risks become more serious? Those early indicators can become the signals your team tracks more closely.

Using Sprout Social Listening, the Atlas team tracks these patterns across channels and spots connections that might be easy to miss when looking at each account on its own. From there, the team can then investigate what’s happening and decide whether a local market needs more guidance.

2. Establish a clear governance framework

Early signals are more useful when teams know what to do with them. Atlas Copco Group created a social media action matrix that sets clear expectations around account ownership, daily content checks and account health scorecards published every six months.

Those shared expectations also strengthen brand safety. When multiple teams and contributors manage social accounts, clear ownership and review processes create more consistency around how teams publish content and respond to potential issues.

Atlas Copco Group uses Tagging in Sprout to organize content by quality and compliance, track which teams are meeting brand standards and identify where additional support is needed.

3. Standardize account health metrics

Atlas Copco Group uses a consistent set of metrics to evaluate brand health in various markets. The team looks at activity, brand compliance, response times and audience engagement together to create a more objective view of performance.

You spend years managing a vibrant, positive brand reputation—nailing the customer experience, delivering great service and watching your reputation thrive. But all it takes is one viral post to make that hard work feel like it’s disappearing overnight.

Even the most experienced marketers face this reality. According to an Axios Harris Poll, 46% of corporate reputations have declined between 2019 and 2025.

Managing brand sentiment can feel overwhelming, but you can take control of your brand’s narrative with a smart corporate reputation management strategy.

What is corporate reputation management?

Corporate reputation management is the practice of proactively influencing and maintaining how the public perceives your brand. This includes monitoring conversations about your company, resolving issues quickly and amplifying positive moments to shape your brand perception.

Corporate reputation management and online reputation management go hand-in-hand. For modern brands, the key aspect that sets them apart is the online focus, which highlights how digital conversations unfolding online shape brand perception and how customers expect you to actively listen on social.

According to a Q2 2026 Sprout Social Pulse Survey, consumers say social is the number one place they hear about a brand crisis first. And when a crisis happens, 64% of consumers say it’s important for a brand to respond publicly on social media rather than through a press release or website statement. This is why social media teams are on the front lines, tasked with protecting and nurturing brand reputation.

A great example of managing a ‘crisis’ online—and getting ahead of the conversation— is the 2018 #ChickenCrises. When KFC ran out of chicken and had to shut down over 750 stores, customers were not happy. Using social listening, the brand noticed the backlash brewing online and quickly addressed the issue with an edgy, self-aware response. They rearranged the letters “KFC” on a chicken bucket to look like a curse word, essentially saying: “We messed up.”

This light-hearted, authentic response defused tension, protected the brand’s reputation and sparked viral trends. And there’s a reason we’re still talking about it eight years later: it’s become an iconic example of a brand apology. It reinforces how vital it is for social media professionals to listen, engage and collaborate with stakeholders to manage reputation challenges to shape brand perception.

Trust impacts everyone from consumers to investors (63% cite it as a critical factor in business-related decisions, according to the Phillips Group). As a marketing leader, your opportunity is to proactively build and protect corporate reputation by engaging with audience conversations and influencing your company’s narrative, wherever it happens.

Why corporate reputation management is important today

Your reputation shapes every part of your business, from winning stakeholder trust to driving sales and building customer loyalty. Because reputation is foundational to brand health, damage to it is one of the biggest risks companies face today.

In highly regulated sectors like financial services, social media acts as an early warning system; a single misunderstood fee structure or service outage can escalate into a compliance nightmare if not addressed with immediate, transparent communication.

The classic Harvard Business Review’s Reputation and Its Risks, notes that 70-80% of the modern economy’s market value comes from “hard-to-assess intangible assets,” like brand equity. This means anything that can hinder your brand—a bad reputation, a crisis—has the power to affect your entire business. Modern data confirms this: Aon’s findings rank reputation damage as the eighth biggest risk to companies worldwide.

But even when you do everything right, outside factors may still influence your reputation. In 2025, a user on Reddit reported that GameStop had charged customers for unreceived products following a $1.4 million merchandise heist.

Rather than letting the issue escalate, GameStop’s social media team acted quickly with a proactive response that clarified that no customer orders were affected. This action helped the company protect its reputation and maintain brand trust.

The team saw that many risks don’t start as large spikes. They show up first as small, repeatable instances like questions, inconsistencies in activity or brand content, and even how local markets experience the brand differently. Each little concern doesn’t seem alarming, but when stacked together, the brand risks start to become clear.

Understanding these patterns through regular listening led them to use social data to push for increased training and governance for internal teams, so they could address inconsistencies early and act before the small moments escalated into larger reputation concerns.
